name: Grace Ito

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Grace. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything you say is confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I do refit carpentry for a small firm called Carrick Interiors, mostly cafés, shops and offices in old buildings in the city centre. This week it's a bakery on Station Street: new counters, stud walls, a bit of panelling, and nothing in a hundred-year-old building is square. Before I leave the house I take a photo of the drawings and ask the AI app on my phone to give me a cut list, then I check it against my own sums on the train. I love the puzzle of old buildings, and I hate the dust, even with the mask.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You said you use the AI every day. How did that start?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My son Haruto showed me two years ago, and I was hooked within a week. Now I use it for cut lists, snag lists, emails to the client, even working out why a glue isn't setting in the cold. The lads at Carrick laugh at me, the old woman with the robot in her pocket. My husband Ken took early retirement from the post office because of his back, so it's my wage that carries us now, plus his small pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hype. I'd be a little disappointed, to be honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's still a good tool, just not the miracle they sold. I'd probably post something in the trade group I'm in, showing how I use it for cut lists, because it does save me half an hour a day. And I'd say thank goodness nobody's job vanished.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it means I carry on as I am, which is all right. I'd still have to get through seven or eight years of dust and ladders. The thing I'd regret is that it never got to the part where it could take the heavy lifting off older people like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep working at Carrick and keep using the app the way I do. I'd probably show a couple of the younger ones how to use it for their own snag lists. And I'd keep putting a bit by each month, we've got about three months of bills saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with a small sigh. Like a film that ends quietly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would you be disappointed, when other people would be relieved?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've seen what it can do in my own small corner, and I wanted it to go further, to help with the heavy, dangerous parts. But I know I'm the odd one out. Most people on site would be pleased it stayed small, and I understand why.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you show it to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kofi, he's twenty-four and he hates paperwork more than anything. If I could get him doing his snag lists by talking into his phone, he'd love me forever. It's a small thing but it makes the day lighter.

S0.say: It's still a good tool, just not the miracle they sold. It saves me half an hour a day on cut lists, and thank goodness nobody's job vanished.
S0.think: I carry on as I am, which is all right, with seven or eight more years of dust and ladders. My regret is that it never got as far as taking the heavy lifting off older people like me.
S0.do: Keeps working at Carrick and keeps using AI for cut lists and snag lists. Teaches a young colleague to do his paperwork by voice and keeps adding to about three months of savings.
S0.feel: Calm, with a small sigh, like a film that ends quietly.
S0.quote: The thing I'd regret is that it never got to the part where it could take the heavy lifting off older people like me.
S0.fieldNote: Unusually for her trade, she'd be slightly disappointed if AI stalled. She wants technology to take on the physical strain of older workers. She is the household's main earner, which matters later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Strong change, but time to adjust. That sounds like the one I'd want, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is our chance, as long as workers get a say in how it's used. I'd push for training paid by the firms and for any time saved to come back to us as shorter weeks, not just bigger profits. I'd say that online and at the union, and I'd mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd do well in this one. I'm already the one at Carrick who uses this stuff. If the drawings come with robot layouts or a machine that marks out walls on the floor, I'd want to be the one who runs it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Carrick, this month, to send me on whatever course there is for layout robots or digital measuring. If they wouldn't pay, I'd pay a bit myself, maybe a few hundred. I'd also go to the union and ask them to start a working group on new tools, so it's not just bosses deciding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit excited. I like a new puzzle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd pay for a course yourself. With three months of savings, is that realistic?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A few hundred, yes. Not thousands. Ken would raise an eyebrow, but he knows I don't waste money on anything else, I haven't bought new clothes in two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone at work you'd worry about in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tony, who's sixty-one and still uses a pencil behind his ear and a folding rule. He's a lovely carpenter but he won't touch a phone. I'd worry he'd be pushed out, and I'd want the union to make sure someone helps him rather than replaces him.

S1.say: This is our chance, as long as workers get a say in how it's used. Firms should pay for training, and time saved should come back to us as shorter weeks, not just bigger profits.
S1.think: I think I'd do well in this one, because I'm already the one at Carrick who uses this stuff. If a machine starts marking out walls on the floor, I want to be the one running it.
S1.do: Asks Carrick this month for a course on layout robots or digital measuring, and pays a few hundred herself if they won't. Asks the union to set up a working group on new tools.
S1.feel: Calm and a bit excited, like facing a new puzzle.
S1.quote: He's a lovely carpenter but he won't touch a phone.
S1.fieldNote: She sees steady change as an opportunity and wants to run the new tools herself. Her progressive views come out as a demand for shorter weeks rather than resistance. She immediately thought of an older colleague who'd struggle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2028. Robots on site too. All right. That's a different story.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a plan for workers right now, a basic income or a wage guarantee, paid for by the companies making the robots. I'd say it everywhere, online, at work, at the union. This would be the time to be loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, in two years even being the robot person doesn't save me. If the machine can do the work and also run itself, they don't need a sixty-year-old woman to watch it. And with Ken's back, my wage is most of what we live on, so this is the one that would actually hurt us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get into whatever robot or AI role exists on sites straight away, applying anywhere, even outside Carrick, to buy a couple of years. I'd save hard, stop the little extras and the gym, and push the union for a deal on wages during the changeover. I'd use the AI to help me write the applications, which is a funny thought.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Clear-headed, but anxious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes for you with only two years of warning, compared with the steady one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the steady one, I'm ahead of the curve and that counts for something. In two years, the curve passes everybody at once, me included. Being early only matters if there's time for it to pay off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Ken that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, love, we need to look at the numbers, and I'd make him a cup of tea first. He'd be worried because he can't go back to work with his back. I'd tell him I'll find something, and I think I would, but I'd be less sure than I sounded.

S2.say: We need a plan for workers right now: a basic income or wage guarantee, paid for by the companies making the robots. This is the time to be loud, online, at work and at the union.
S2.think: In two years even being the robot person doesn't save me, because a machine that runs itself doesn't need a sixty-year-old woman watching it. With Ken's back, my wage is most of what we live on.
S2.do: Applies straight away for any robot or AI role on sites, inside or outside Carrick, to buy a couple of years. Saves hard by dropping extras and the gym, and pushes the union for a wage deal during the changeover.
S2.quote: Being early only matters if there's time for it to pay off.
S2.fieldNote: Her adaptability helps her stay clear-headed, but she knows it buys little time in the fastest picture. The household depends on her wage because of Ken's back. She admitted she'd sound more confident to Ken than she'd feel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. I'd be sixty-three. That's a bit more room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same thing, the gains need sharing, but I'd add that five years is enough time to get it right. I'd say retrain people now, not when the robots arrive. I'd be at the union pushing for a training fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, five years is enough for me to be useful through the change. I'd learn to set up and fix the site robots, and those jobs might last until I'm sixty-three. After that I'd retire, maybe a little early, and I'd be at peace with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd do a proper course in robotics on building sites, or whatever the college offers, evenings if I have to. I'd keep saving and use the AI every day to learn faster. And I'd talk to a couple of older trades about whether we could set up a small team that hires out a robot and runs it, so we own the thing instead of it owning us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more hopeful than scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A small team that owns the robot. Would you really do that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to. Like a co-op, a few of us putting money in, sharing the work and the profit. Whether we'd get the money is another matter, a robot isn't a drill, but I'd at least look into it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra time give you that two years didn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time to learn the thing properly instead of grabbing at it. In two years I'm applying for anything. In five years I can plan, and I'm good at plans when I've got time to make them.

S3.say: The gains need sharing, and five years is enough time to get it right. Retrain people now, not when the robots arrive, and set up a proper training fund.
S3.think: Five years is enough for me to be useful through the change. I could set up and fix the site robots until sixty-three, then retire a little early and be at peace with it.
S3.do: Enrols this year in a college course on robotics in construction, evenings if needed, using AI daily to learn faster. Looks into a small co-op of older trades that would own and hire out a site robot.
S3.feel: Uneasy, but more hopeful than scared.
S3.quote: So we own the thing instead of it owning us.
S3.fieldNote: With five years her plans become ambitious: a co-op owning a robot, which blends her progressive values with her appetite for new tools. She was honest about not knowing whether they could raise the money. Time turns grabbing into planning for her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2036. I'd be sixty-eight, so retired, unless I'm still having fun with robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty to do this fairly, so if it goes wrong, it's a choice somebody made. I'd want laws on sharing the gains, shorter weeks, a decent pension for everyone. I'd vote for that and campaign a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, this one's fine for me. I'd ride the change for a few years, maybe teach younger people how to work with the machines, then retire on time. My worry is Mia, my daughter, who works in a call centre, that job will be gone way before 2036.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep working at Carrick, keep learning, and maybe do some teaching at the college in my last years. I'd talk to Mia about moving into something with people, maybe care work or teaching. And I'd volunteer for whatever campaign was pushing for a fair deal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm for me, worried for Mia. Mostly hopeful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Mia, exactly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, you've got ten years but your job hasn't, so start now. She'd roll her eyes, she always does when I talk about AI. But I'd send her links every week until she listened.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change your retirement plans in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd retire about sixty-six, like I planned. Maybe I'd do a day a week teaching after that, if they let me. Ken would want me home, though, he says I talk about robots in my sleep.

S4.say: Ten years is plenty to do this fairly, so if it goes wrong, someone chose that. I'd vote and campaign for laws on sharing the gains, shorter weeks and a decent pension for everyone.
S4.think: This one's fine for me: I'd ride the change, maybe teach younger people, then retire on time. My worry is Mia in her call centre job, which will be gone long before 2036.
S4.do: Carries on at Carrick, keeps learning and may teach at the college in her last working years. Urges her daughter to move into people-focused work and volunteers for a fair-transition campaign.
S4.feel: Calm for herself, worried for her daughter, and mostly hopeful.
S4.quote: I'd say, you've got ten years but your job hasn't, so start now.
S4.fieldNote: The decade-long picture leaves her personally secure and energised. Her concern shifts to her daughter's call-centre job. She would put her energy into campaigning and teaching.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. In the others, being someone who picks things up quickly actually pays off, but in two years nobody's quick enough. And it's my wage we live on, with Ken's back. What would help is a wage guarantee during the changeover, paid for by the companies with the robots, and training money that reaches people like me before the jobs go, not after.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether I'd want to own any of it. Everybody assumes workers just get replaced or kept. I'd like to own a bit of the machine that does my job. That's the question I'd want you asking everyone.

headlineQuote: I'd like to own a bit of the machine that does my job.
portrait: Grace Ito is a 58-year-old refit carpenter at Carrick Interiors who uses AI every day for cut lists and snag lists, and whose wage carries the household since her husband Ken retired with a bad back. She'd be slightly disappointed if AI stalled and sees steady change as a chance to run new site machines. The two-year AGI picture makes her anxious, because being early doesn't help if everyone is overtaken at once. With five or ten years she plans boldly, including a co-op of older trades owning a robot. She wants workers to own part of the machines, not just be replaced or kept.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because nobody can adapt fast enough and her household depends on her wage.
whatWouldHelp: A wage guarantee during the changeover paid for by the companies with the robots, and training money that arrives before the jobs go.
